On the night of the first frost, Maren took her daughter by the hand and walked her out of Carrow Ford, past the last fence post, past the last lamp, and into the Ashen Reach, the scorched valley where the dragons hunt. Ailis was nine years old. She did not ask why. Her mother had been strange for weeks, ever since the tax-reeve Osric had moved into the toll-house and started calling the ford charter his future.

At the edge of the burned trees, Maren knelt and pressed a small brass lantern into her daughter's hands. It was the lantern from the toll-gate, the one Ailis had polished every evening since she was tall enough to reach the hook. Wait here, Maren said. Keep it lit. I will come back for you before the moon is high. Then she straightened the high collar of the girl's coat, the way she always did, so that the rust-red whorl on her collarbone stayed hidden, and she walked away without turning around.

Ailis waited. The moon rose, and passed its height, and began to fall. The lantern burned lower. She pulled her knees up inside her coat and counted the stars between the branches, the way her father had taught her before he died, because counting was something to do with her mind that was not crying. Somewhere far off, something enormous moved through the dark, and the dead branches creaked under the weight of it. She told herself it was the wind. She told herself a great many things, because the alternative was the one thought she could not hold: that her mother had not lost her. Her mother had left her.

She remembered the argument through the kitchen wall two nights before. Osric's voice, low and patient, the voice he used on travellers who could not pay the toll. The charter passes by blood, he had said. Only to the wardens' line. And that mark on the girl is the wardens' mark, whatever you pretend. If the crown's inquisitors ever see it, they will take the house, the ford, everything. Her mother had not answered. That silence, Ailis understood now, had been the answer.

Near midnight the air changed. The frost on the ground began to steam. A shadow slid across the stars, and then the ground shook as something landed at the far end of the clearing, so heavy that the lantern flame leaned sideways. Ailis did not scream. She had always been the kind of child who went very still when frightened, and she went still now, holding the lantern in both hands like a shield that could not possibly protect her.

The dragon walked into the circle of light. She was grey, the grey of cold ash, with a band of dull bronze wrapped around her left horn. Her eyes were the size of cart wheels, and they were looking directly at the girl. Ailis could smell smoke and river stone and something older, like the inside of a church. The dragon lowered her head, slowly, until the great nostrils were close enough to stir the loose end of her copper-red braid.

Then she stopped. She did not open her jaws. Instead she turned her head very slightly, as if listening. And Ailis felt it, under the collar her mother had straightened: the whorl on her collarbone had grown warm, warm as a hand laid there by someone who meant to stay. The dragon breathed out, long and low, and lowered her head further, all the way down, until it rested on the frozen ground at the girl's feet.
